newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia c.bank sold T-bills to soak up excess money.
newsitem.headline: Russia c.bank sold T-bills to soak up excess money.

text.p: Russia's central bank has been selling government securities recently from its portfolio to soak up excess money generated by heavy currency inflows, a senior central banker said on Tuesday.
The portfolio, details of which are not usually disclosed, shrank by 3.5-4.0 trillion roubles ($600-700 million) in June- July, First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told Reuters.

Money supply in the first half of this year had grown faster than forecast by the central bank, and monetary policy had been largely determined by the finance ministry's significant currency inflows, he said.

The ministry raised large sums through Eurobond issues, World Bank loans, and an International Monetary Fund loan tranche. Most of these funds were converted to roubles which were then bought by the central bank with T-bills.
"Because of these external influences we had to conduct an active policy of sterilising money by selling our portfolio of government securities," Aleksashenko said.

"It has to be said that the portfolio fell substantially. During June and July we have sold...about 3.5-4.0 trillion roubles in a month and a half. In other words we have absorbed about $800 million," he said.
The central bank has not yet issued money supply data for the first half year. But as of June 1 M2 money supply was 339.4 trillion roubles, a rise of 15.0 percent since January 1.
Aleksashenko said there was no reason to believe that the increase in money supply would feed through into inflation, which has slowed every month since mid-1995.
Russian financial markets had already absorbed these funds and Treasury bill rates were steady while overnight rouble funds were close to zero, he said.
The central bank would pursue a restrained monetary policy in the second half of the year, Aleksashenko said.
"We expect that the finance ministry will not have such large currency inflows and monetary policy will be determined by our steps rather than the budget," he said.
